examples.question_text: The revenue from selling $x$ hundred items is $R(x)=200x-10x^{2}$ thousand dollars, for $0\le x\le15$. Find the number of items sold and the maximum revenue in dollars.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}R'(x)&=200-20x\\200-20x&=0\\x&=10\end{aligned}$
Since $R''(x)=-20<0$, the stationary point is a local maximum.
Compare it with the endpoints:
$\begin{aligned}R(0)&=0\\R(10)&=1000\\R(15)&=750\end{aligned}$
Selling $1000$ items gives the maximum revenue of $\$1\,000\,000$.

examples.question_text: A quantity is modelled by $F(t)=t^{3}-9t^{2}+24t$, for $0\le t\le7$. Find its global maximum and minimum values.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}F'(t)&=3t^{2}-18t+24\\3(t-2)(t-4)&=0\\t&=2\text{ or }4\\F''(t)&=6t-18\end{aligned}$
Both stationary points lie in the domain. Since $F''(2)=-6<0$ and $F''(4)=6>0$, they are a local maximum and a local minimum respectively.
Compare all candidate values:
$\begin{aligned}F(0)&=0\\F(2)&=20\\F(4)&=16\\F(7)&=70\end{aligned}$
The global maximum is $70$ at $t=7$, and the global minimum is $0$ at $t=0$. The local maximum is not the global maximum.

examples.question_text: The average cost is $A(x)=2x+\dfrac{32}{x}+5$ dollars, for $1\le x\le8$. Find the minimum average cost.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}A'(x)&=2-\frac{32}{x^{2}}\\2-\frac{32}{x^{2}}&=0\\x^{2}&=16\\x&=4\end{aligned}$
Only the positive root lies in the domain. Since $A''(x)=\dfrac{64}{x^{3}}>0$, it gives a local minimum.
$\begin{aligned}A(1)&=39\\A(4)&=21\\A(8)&=25\end{aligned}$
The minimum average cost is $\$21$.

examples.question_text: A truck travels $240$ km at a constant speed of $v$ km/h. Its hourly cost is $\left(25+\dfrac{v^{2}}{100}\right)$ dollars, for $20\le v\le80$. Find the speed that minimises the trip cost and the minimum cost.
examples.solution_text:
The trip takes $\dfrac{240}{v}$ hours.
$\begin{aligned}C(v)&=\left(25+\frac{v^{2}}{100}\right)\frac{240}{v}\\&=\frac{6000}{v}+\frac{12v}{5}\\C'(v)&=-\frac{6000}{v^{2}}+\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}$
Set the derivative equal to zero:
$\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{5}v^{2}&=6000\\v^{2}&=2500\\v&=50\end{aligned}$
Since $C''(v)=\dfrac{12\,000}{v^{3}}>0$, this is a local minimum.
$\begin{aligned}C(20)&=348\\C(50)&=240\\C(80)&=267\end{aligned}$
The minimum trip cost is $\$240$, at $50$ km/h.

Let $x$ be each perpendicular side and $y$ the side parallel to the wall.
$\begin{aligned}2x+y&=64\\y&=64-2x\\A(x)&=x(64-2x)\\&=64x-2x^{2}\end{aligned}$
Positive side lengths require $0<x<32$.
$\begin{aligned}A'(x)&=64-4x\\64-4x&=0\\x&=16\\A''(x)&=-4<0\end{aligned}$
The area approaches $0$ at both domain boundaries, so the stationary point gives the global maximum.
$\begin{aligned}y&=64-2(16)\\&=32\\A(16)&=512\end{aligned}$
The dimensions are $16$ m perpendicular to the wall and $32$ m parallel to it. The maximum area is $512$ m$^{2}$.

The box has height $x$ and base dimensions $30-2x$ and $12-2x$ cm, so $0<x<6$.
$\begin{aligned}V(x)&=x(30-2x)(12-2x)\\&=360x-84x^{2}+4x^{3}\\V'(x)&=360-168x+12x^{2}\end{aligned}$
Set the derivative equal to zero:
$\begin{aligned}12(x^{2}-14x+30)&=0\\x&=7\pm\sqrt{19}\end{aligned}$
Only $x=7-\sqrt{19}$ lies in the domain.
$\begin{aligned}V''(x)&=24x-168\\V''(7-\sqrt{19})&=-24\sqrt{19}<0\end{aligned}$
The volume approaches $0$ at both domain boundaries, so this is the global maximum.
$\begin{aligned}V(7-\sqrt{19})&=152\sqrt{19}-56\\&\approx606.55\end{aligned}$
Cut squares of side $7-\sqrt{19}\approx2.64$ cm. The maximum volume is $606.55$ cm$^{3}$, to two decimal places.

Let the poster dimensions be $x$ and $y$ cm. Then $y=\dfrac{576}{x}$.
$\begin{aligned}A(x)&=(x-6)\left(\frac{576}{x}-6\right)\\&=612-6x-\frac{3456}{x}\end{aligned}$
The photograph must have positive dimensions, so $6<x<96$.
$\begin{aligned}A'(x)&=-6+\frac{3456}{x^{2}}\\-6+\frac{3456}{x^{2}}&=0\\x^{2}&=576\\x&=24\end{aligned}$
Since $A''(x)=-\dfrac{6912}{x^{3}}<0$ throughout the domain, the stationary point is a maximum. The area approaches $0$ at both boundaries.
$\begin{aligned}y&=\frac{576}{24}\\&=24\\A(24)&=(24-6)^{2}\\&=324\end{aligned}$
The maximum photograph area is $324$ cm$^{2}$.

By Pythagoras, the rowing distance is $\sqrt{16+x^{2}}$ km. The walking distance is $10-x$ km.
$\begin{aligned}T(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{16+x^{2}}}{3}+\frac{10-x}{5},\qquad0\le x\le10\\T'(x)&=\frac{x}{3\sqrt{16+x^{2}}}-\frac15\end{aligned}$
Set the derivative equal to zero:
$\begin{aligned}5x&=3\sqrt{16+x^{2}}\\25x^{2}&=9(16+x^{2})\\16x^{2}&=144\\x&=3\end{aligned}$
The nonnegative root satisfies the original equation. The derivative is negative for $0\le x<3$ and positive for $3<x\le10$, so the time decreases then increases.
$\begin{aligned}T(0)&=\frac{10}{3}\\T(3)&=\frac53+\frac75=\frac{46}{15}\\T(10)&=\frac{\sqrt{116}}3\end{aligned}$
The smallest candidate value is $T(3)$. She should land $3$ km from $A$ towards $B$.

$\begin{aligned}A(x)&=\frac12xy\\&=\frac{x^{2}}{2(x-2)},\qquad x>2\end{aligned}$
Use the quotient rule:
$\begin{aligned}A'(x)&=\frac{2x(x-2)-x^{2}}{2(x-2)^{2}}\\&=\frac{x(x-4)}{2(x-2)^{2}}\end{aligned}$
The stationary roots are $0$ and $4$; only $4$ lies in the domain. The derivative is negative for $2<x<4$ and positive for $x>4$, so the area decreases then increases. Also, $A(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to2^{+}$ or $x\to\infty$.
$A(4)=\dfrac{16}{2(2)}=4$.
The global minimum area is $4$ square units.

examples.question_text: A quantity is $Q(t)=\dfrac{60t}{t^{2}+9}$, for $1\le t\le6$. Find the value of $t$ that maximises $Q$.
examples.solution_text:
Use the quotient rule:
$\begin{aligned}Q'(t)&=\frac{60(t^{2}+9)-60t(2t)}{(t^{2}+9)^{2}}\\&=\frac{60(9-t^{2})}{(t^{2}+9)^{2}}\end{aligned}$
The derivative is zero at $t=\pm3$; only $t=3$ lies in the domain. Its denominator is positive, so $Q'(t)>0$ for $1\le t<3$ and $Q'(t)<0$ for $3<t\le6$. This gives a local maximum.
Compare the candidate values:
$\begin{aligned}Q(1)&=6\\Q(3)&=10\\Q(6)&=8\end{aligned}$
The quantity is greatest at $t=3$.

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$ metres, for $0\le t\le5$ seconds. Find its greatest distance from the origin.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}s'(t)&=3t^{2}-12t+9\\3(t-1)(t-3)&=0\\t&=1\text{ or }3\\s''(t)&=6t-12\end{aligned}$
Since $s''(1)=-6<0$ and $s''(3)=6>0$, the stationary points are a local maximum and a local minimum respectively.
Compare the displacement magnitudes at the stationary points and endpoints:
$\begin{aligned}|s(0)|&=0\\|s(1)|&=4\\|s(3)|&=0\\|s(5)|&=20\end{aligned}$
Here $s(t)=t(t-3)^{2}\ge0$ throughout the domain. The greatest distance from the origin is $20$ m, reached at $t=5$ seconds.

examples.derivation: R'=200-20x gives x=10; R''=-20. Candidate revenues are 0, 1000 and 750 thousand dollars. Thus 1000 items yield $1,000,000.
F'=3(t-2)(t-4), with F''=6t-18. Values at t=0,2,4,7 are 0,20,16,70. Global maximum 70 and minimum 0 occur at the endpoints.
A'=2-32/x² vanishes at admissible x=4; A''=64/x³>0. Values at x=1,4,8 are 39,21,25, giving minimum cost $21.
Multiplying hourly cost by 240/v gives C=6000/v+12v/5. C'=0 gives v=50, and C''=12000/v³>0. Candidate costs are $348, $240 and $267.
2x+y=64 gives A=64x-2x² on 0<x<32. A'=64-4x gives x=16; A''=-4. Boundary areas tend to zero. Hence y=32 and maximum area is 512 m². Diagram labels match the constraint.

V=x(30-2x)(12-2x)=360x-84x²+4x³ on 0<x<6. V'=12(x²-14x+30), giving 7±√19; only 7-√19 is admissible. V''=-24√19 there, and boundary volumes tend to zero. Substitution gives 152√19-56≈606.55 cm³. The planar corner-cut diagram preserves the givens.

xy=576 gives A=(x-6)(576/x-6)=612-6x-3456/x on 6<x<96. A'=0 gives x=24; A''=-6912/x³<0. Boundary areas tend to zero. Thus y=24 and photograph area is 324 cm². Diagram margins and dimension labels agree.

Pythagoras and distance/speed give T=√(16+x²)/3+(10-x)/5. T'=0 gives 5x=3√(16+x²), hence x=3. T' changes from negative to positive. Candidate times are 10/3, 46/15 and √116/3 hours, so landing 3 km from A minimises time. Diagram relationships agree.

A=x²/[2(x-2)] on x>2. The quotient rule gives A'=x(x-4)/[2(x-2)²]. Only x=4 is admissible; derivative signs are negative then positive, and both boundary limits are infinite. A(4)=4 square units. The illustrative line passes through P(2,1) and the labelled intercepts.
The quotient rule gives Q'=60(9-t²)/(t²+9)². Only t=3 is admissible, with positive then negative derivative signs. Values at t=1,3,6 are 6,10,8, so t=3 maximises Q.
s'=3(t-1)(t-3), with s''=6t-12. Candidate displacement magnitudes at t=0,1,3,5 are 0,4,0,20. Since s=t(t-3)²≥0, greatest distance is 20 m at t=5.
